claims.text: Optimizing grain orientation in an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy coating facilitates coherent slip transmission across phase boundaries.
Coherent slip transmission across FCC/BCC phase boundaries limits localized strain accumulation.
Limiting localized strain accumulation suppresses shear-band formation.
Suppressing localized strain and shear bands retards creep deformation during continuous high-temperature loading.
The conventionally processed baseline coating has random grain orientations and uncontrolled grain size.
Random grain orientations produce variable slip transmission across FCC/BCC interfaces.
Directional solidification or tailored thermomechanical processing can induce preferential grain alignment in the coating.
The proposed processing will produce aligned slip systems and reduced misorientation at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Concurrent control of grain growth will produce a stable, refined grain-size distribution.
Controlled crystallographic alignment promotes homogeneous slip transmission across FCC/BCC phase boundaries.
Homogeneous slip transmission prevents localized strain accumulation and inhibits creep-producing shear bands.
Relative to the random-orientation baseline, an aligned coating will have a lower steady-state creep rate.
Relative to the baseline, an aligned coating will have a more uniform strain field.
Relative to the baseline, an aligned coating will develop a lower density of shear bands during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
Random grain orientation and uncontrolled grain-size evolution promote localized slip and shear-band formation, accelerating creep.
The proposed orientation-controlled mechanism is expected to be most effective under sustained loading at 600–700°C.
At lower temperatures or under different stress states, creep mechanisms other than controlled slip transmission may dominate.
Grain coarsening may occur during processing or service.
Differences in grain size could confound attribution of creep resistance to grain orientation.
